name: Recomp

card.summary: Body recomposition: losing fat and gaining muscle at the same time, mostly discussed for beginners and skinny-fat lifters.
card.note: Forum threads also discuss drug-assisted recomp, which carries separate risks.

quick.overview:
Recomp, short for body recomposition, is the attempt to lose fat and add muscle at the same time, usually by eating near maintenance with resistance training and high protein. Forum posters most often discuss it for skinny-fat people who want a leaner look without a separate bulk and cut.

Threads range from natural diet and training plans to drug-assisted approaches. Some users advise against it and recommend alternating phases instead.
quick.mechanism: Calories are held around maintenance or a slight deficit while lifting and protein intake support muscle retention or gain. Forum users calculate calorie and macro targets week by week.
quick.risks: The sources examined contain no clinical studies. Appetite-suppressing or fat-loss drugs mentioned alongside recomp in forums carry their own medical risks and are not endorsed here. Slow, hard-to-measure progress is the main practical caveat users cite.

chain: Resistance training with high protein and a modest calorie target
Muscle is added or kept while fat is lost
Lower body fat with more visible shape through the face, shoulders and torso
angle.text: Recomp users train with weights, eat high protein and hold calories near maintenance or in a small deficit, aiming to swap fat for muscle in one phase. The result they seek is a visibly leaner, more filled-out physique and a more defined face without cycling between bulking and cutting.

lead: Recomp, short for body recomposition, is the attempt to reduce body fat and build or keep muscle at the same time, in contrast with alternating a bulk and a cut.[1][2] People pursue it to look leaner and more muscular without a long fat-gain phase and without large swings in body weight. The visible payoff they describe is a more defined jawline and face, broader-looking shoulders and a flatter midsection from the same bodyweight.

It is discussed on looksmaxxing and lifting forums mainly in relation to skinny-fat bodies, where a person has low muscle and relatively high fat, and by beginners, returning lifters and people with higher body fat, the groups in which research and trainers say recomposition is most pronounced.[2][6][10] Posters ask for week-by-week calorie and macronutrient plans, discuss modest deficits with intermittent fasting and high protein, and debate whether recomp is a sensible approach compared with a dedicated bulk or cut.[2][3]

The core ingredients are the same in most accounts: progressive resistance training, high protein, and calories held near maintenance or in a small deficit. Research reviews describe resistance training with about 1.6 to 2.4 g of protein per kg of body weight per day as the most consistent recomposition strategy.[6] A 2016 randomised trial in young men found that a high-protein diet during a large energy deficit with intense training produced greater lean mass gain and fat loss than a lower-protein diet.[11]

paras: Recomp aims to change body composition without large changes in weight. It is typically contrasted with bulking in a surplus and cutting in a deficit, which Wikipedia describes as the usual alternating phases in bodybuilding.[1] Because muscle is denser than fat, the scale may barely move while waist, face and shape change, so practitioners usually track progress with measurements, photos and strength rather than weight alone.

Related terms in the same vocabulary include skinny-fat (low muscle, moderate fat), lean bulk (a small surplus intended to limit fat gain), cut, and maintenance calories, the intake at which weight stays steady. A calculator posted to Hacker News in 2026 offered maintenance-calorie estimates for lean bulks, cuts and body recomp.[7]

sections.h: Bulking, cutting and where recomp fits
paras: Bodybuilding references describe an off-season of net positive energy balance, called bulking, followed by a contest-preparation phase of net negative balance, called cutting.[1] Clean bulking tries to add muscle with little fat gain, while dirty bulking uses a large surplus and typically needs a harder cut afterwards.[1] Cutting is described as starting around 12 to 14 weeks before a show, and a larger deficit speeds weight loss but raises the risk of losing muscle.[1]

The same article gives indicative muscle-gain rates: novices may gain roughly 4 to 7 kg of muscle a year in their first two years, falling to 2 to 7 kg a year and then 1 to 5 kg a year after five years of training.[1] Recomp is often presented as most plausible where gains are fastest, in people new to lifting or returning after a break, and the faster pace of early gains is one reason advocates offer for it.

Wikipedia's article on muscle hypertrophy adds that frequency, intensity and volume all affect growth, that progressive overload is central, that early strength gains are largely neural, and that genetics account for a substantial share of variation in muscle mass.[12] Supporters of phased bulking and cutting argue that a surplus gives the clearest signal for muscle growth, while recomp supporters argue that a person who is not very lean can get most of the same effect without a surplus.

Gaining muscle usually needs resistance training and enough protein, and losing fat needs lower energy intake than expenditure; recomp tries to do both at once. A 2026 structured review in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition reported that resistance training with about 1.6 to 2.4 g of protein per kg of body weight per day is the most consistent recomposition strategy, with larger effects in untrained and higher-adiposity adults.[6]

The ISSN position stand on protein and exercise states that 1.4 to 2.0 g/kg/day is sufficient for most exercising people to build or keep muscle, that 2.3 to 3.1 g/kg/day may be needed to retain lean mass in resistance-trained people during hypocaloric periods, and that intakes above 3.0 g/kg/day may promote fat loss in resistance-trained people.[5] Wikipedia's bodybuilding article notes that protein recommendations vary and that it is unclear whether enough fat-free mass can be kept during cutting for the process to be worthwhile.[1]

A 2023 review by Janssen, Van Every and Phillips on very low-calorie diets concluded that resistance training should be the priority for preserving muscle during energy restriction, with adequate protein as a secondary measure.[13]

Descriptions on forums and in training literature converge on a few elements. Training is typically progressive resistance work several days a week.[2][3] Protein is set high and spread across meals, calories are held near maintenance or slightly below.[3][6]

Users report tracking weight trends, waist circumference, progress photos and lifts over months rather than weeks. Some use intermittent fasting windows as a way to manage intake; one poster combined a small daily deficit with intermittent fasting and about 1.2 g of protein per kg and reported losing 13 pounds in three months.[3] A 2021 randomised trial in resistance-trained adults found that flexible and rigid dieting produced similar fat loss over ten weeks at a calorie deficit of about 20 percent.[14]

Recomp has its own forum threads, calculators and calorie-target discussions. T Nation members ask about recomp calorie targets, expectations and whether recomposition is possible after two years of training, and threads there also discuss drug-assisted recomposition.[15][16][17] A 2026 Hacker News post presented a calculator for maintenance calories covering lean bulks, cuts and body recomp.[7]

On looksmaxxing forums, threads range from guides arguing against recomposing for skinny-fat people to requests for week-by-week plans and posts about adding fat-loss drugs while bulking.[2][3][4] The term sits within a wider vocabulary of skinny-fat, lean bulk, cut and maintenance that physique communities use to plan changes in appearance.

One long guide addressed to skinny-fat and overweight people argues against recomposing and recommends an alternative sequence, and invites readers who are not in those groups to read it anyway.[2] Another poster seeking a plan to reach 10 percent body fat naturally describes a 350 kcal daily deficit with intermittent fasting and about 1.2 g of protein per kg, losing 13 pounds in three months.[3]

A third thread asks whether L-carnitine and retatrutide can allow recomposition while bulking. Replies say retatrutide mainly suppresses appetite, making it hard to bulk on, while another says fat burning can occur if intake stays above maintenance.[4]

Related approaches include lean bulking, mini-cuts, intermittent fasting, high-protein dieting, and cut-then-bulk sequencing. Competitive physique athletes also study what happens after a cut: a 2026 study of 19 natural physique athletes tracked body composition from about 21 weeks before competition through 12 weeks after. Fat-free mass at 12 weeks exceeded baseline by about 1.6 kg while fat mass was not clearly different from baseline.[18]

Younger men. In a 2016 randomised trial, 40 young men followed a diet about 40 percent below energy requirements while doing resistance and interval training six days a week for four weeks. The group on 2.4 g/kg/day of protein gained 1.2 kg of lean mass and lost 4.8 kg of fat mass, compared with 0.1 kg and 3.5 kg in the group on 1.2 g/kg/day.[11]

Women and older adults. Randomised and retrospective studies have examined recomposition in particular groups, mostly women and older adults. A 2022 analysis in Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise of 130 older women over 24 weeks of resistance training grouped participants by protein intake: skeletal muscle mass rose 2.3 percent in the low-protein group and 5.4 and 5.1 percent in the moderate and higher groups, while fat mass fell 1.7, 3.7 and 3.1 percent, with recomposition scores higher in the moderate and high groups.[8] A 2023 retrospective analysis of 99 older women found the group with the lowest baseline fat mass showed greater positive recomposition over 24 weeks of resistance training, with strength gains similar across groups.[10] A 16-week randomised trial of 96 postmenopausal women found functional and combined training both increased lean mass from week 8 and reduced fat percentage from week 12 without changing body mass.[8]

Diet and exercise combined. A 12-month randomised trial of 439 sedentary postmenopausal women found weight change of -8.5 percent with diet, -2.4 percent with aerobic exercise and -10.8 percent with both, with lean mass not reported in its abstract.[9]
Gap. No published trial has compared recomposition with phased bulking and cutting for visible appearance outcomes in young men.

timeline.event: US National Academy of Medicine era of formal macronutrient guidance on protein; bodybuilding phases of bulking and cutting already standard practice.[1]
A 12-month randomised trial in 439 postmenopausal women compares diet, exercise and both.[9]
Randomised trial finds higher protein during a large deficit with intense training gives greater lean gain and fat loss in young men.[11]
ISSN position stand sets protein ranges for exercise, including for hypocaloric periods.[5]
Randomised trial compares flexible and rigid dieting in resistance-trained adults.[14]
Analysis of 130 older women links moderate-to-high protein intake with larger recomposition during resistance training.[8]
Review stresses resistance training and protein for preserving muscle on very low-calorie diets.[13]
ISSN-affiliated review sets out mechanisms and practical algorithms for simultaneous muscle gain and fat loss.[6]

lore.intro: Recomp is a recurring question among skinny-fat users who want to look leaner and more muscular without a long bulk and cut.[2][3]

claims.claim: Skinny-fat people should not recomp and should bulk or cut instead
claims.believers: A guide titled to warn against body recomp argues for a different path for skinny-fat and overweight people.[2]
claims.experts: No published trial in the sources examined compares recomp with phased bulking and cutting for appearance outcomes.

claims.claim: Drugs plus L-carnitine allow recomp even while bulking
claims.believers: A poster reports noticeable facial debloating after about ten days of L-carnitine and plans to add retatrutide.[4]
claims.experts: No clinical studies on this combination for appearance were found; replies in the same thread note retatrutide mainly suppresses appetite.[4]

claims.claim: A small daily deficit with high protein can lose fat while keeping muscle
claims.believers: A poster describes losing 13 lb over three months on a roughly 350 kcal deficit and asks for an exact plan.[3]
claims.experts: Bodybuilding encyclopedias say larger deficits raise muscle-loss risk, and describe high protein as part of muscle-preserving cuts.[1]

claims.claim: Recomp works best for beginners and returning lifters.
claims.believers: Posters and trainers say early gains come fast enough that muscle can grow even at maintenance calories.[2][3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia gives the highest muscle-gain rates for novices,[1] and the 2026 review reports larger recomposition effects in untrained and higher-adiposity adults.[6]

claims.claim: High protein is the key to losing fat while keeping or gaining muscle.
claims.believers: Users set protein targets well above basic recommendations during a cut.[3]
claims.experts: A 2016 randomised trial found 2.4 g/kg/day produced greater lean gain and fat loss than 1.2 g/kg/day in a large deficit.[11] The ISSN position stand gives higher ranges for hypocaloric periods.[5]

claims.claim: The scale will not move, so track mirror and measurements instead.
claims.believers: Posters describe judging progress by photos and waist size.[3]
claims.experts: The reviewed studies report changes in fat mass and lean mass measured by body composition tools rather than body weight alone.[8][10]

claims.claim: Recomp is a poor choice for skinny-fat people, who should bulk or cut first.
claims.believers: One guide argues skinny-fat people should follow a different sequence.[2]
claims.experts: No published trial in young men compares recomp with phased bulking and cutting for appearance outcomes.
